blocks.text: To these has been added in our own time Aurivillius, who in his Dissertation on the names of the animals that are read in Esaj. XIII, 21. § 4 (in his Dissertations, edited by Michaelis, p. 302–305) contends that the word בת יענה signifies little owls, with almost the same arguments that Fuller once brought forward, but which have already been sufficiently refuted by Bochart. The same opinion is also defended by Oedmann, Vermischte Sammlungen vol. 3, ch. 3, p. 35 ff.
Athenaeus book 5, ch. 7. Eustathius on the Iliad β′ [2].

Oedmann objects (3, p. 41) that the ostrich's harshness towards its young cannot be proved by any adequate testimony. This I leave open for now. It is enough that the Hebrews held that opinion; and that they did is sufficiently clear from the passage of Job that Bochart cites. Nor has Oedmann himself demonstrated that the eagle owls, which he thinks are meant, neglect their young.
Oedmann has rehashed this very point, loc. cit. But Bochart meets this doubt in such a way that I see nothing that can rightly be objected to him.

But Johannes de Laet is speaking of the struthio Rhea Linn., which is peculiar to the New World alone, a bird wholly different in kind from the ostrich, as Oedmann rightly observes, 3, p. 38, 39. Nevertheless, in place of the passage of Johannes de Laet one may substitute Shaw, Travels p. 390, German trans., where he describes the varied voice of ostriches, sometimes mournful, howling, drawing deep sighs. And Oedmann, 3, p. 38, has undeservedly cast suspicion on Shaw's testimony, which stands in the way of his opinion.
The testimonies of more recent writers have been brought forward by Michaelis in the Supplemm. 4, p. 1126 ff.

Since for the Arabs وَعْنَةٌ [waʿnah] is hard ground, Paulus, in the Clavis Iesaiae p. 96, supposes that the same meaning lies in the Hebrew יענה, so that בת יענה would denote in general animals that live in desert places. But that some certain and definite animal is signified by this expression is clearly apparent from the passages in which בת יענה is listed among individual species of birds, such as Levit. XI, 16. Deut. XIV, 15., not to mention the ancient translators, who with one mind understand the ostrich, and whose agreement carries much weight with me. The meaning of the word יענה that Paulus brings us from Arabia, however, we gratefully accept. For if יענה meant desert for the Hebrews, then this Hebrew name of the ostrich, בת יענה, daughter of the desert, will be not very unlike ابو الصحاري [abū al-ṣaḥārī] father of the deserts, which is one of the names of the ostrich among the Arabs, according to Damir, cited by Bochart below, Chapter 15, p. 233. J. D. Michaelis had arrived at a similar thought; his words in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1127 are these: "it also occurred to me to relate the word יענה to יען, Arabic وَعَنَ [waʿana], which denotes barren and whitish ground, just as the ostrich is called by the Arabs امّ البيض [umm al-bayḍ], perhaps mother of the whitish desert [rather mother of eggs, see Damir below, p. 233]." He is, however, more inclined to the view that בת יענה properly signifies daughter of misery, and that this name was given to the ostrich because it lives in poor deserts that lack even water.
